The package `vgi4bio` contains functions for the combined analysis of opportunistic and standardized dataset to estimate relative abundances of multiple species, and habitat preferences.  
  


# The Aquitaine data set

The Aquitaine dataset is used to illustrate several methods. It is stored as a list and contains the data used to develop the models in @Giraud2015 and @Coron2018. 

```{r, eval=F}
library(vgi4bio)
data(Aquitaine)
```

The data.frame Aquitaine contains the following variables (for a complete list of variables, see the suggested citation):

*Species*: this variable stores the code of the bird species. This code is formed by concatenating the first three letters of the genus and the first three letters of the species (see the first column of Table 1 in the main text);  

*Site*: this variable stores the code of the 63 ACT sites used for the model fit;  

*Species\_in\_ACT*: 1 if the species is monitored by the ACT programme, 0 otherwise (for these species, *X\_ACT* is a structural zero, not an absence);

*Effort\_ACT*: the number of listening points-years implemented in the ACT program for the site stored in the variable *Site*;  

*X\_ACT*: the abundance of the species stored in the variable *Species* detected in the site stored in the
  variable *Site* by the ACT program;  

*X\_LPO*: the abundance of the species stored in the variable *Species* detected in the site stored in the variable *Site* by the opportunistic LPO program;


# Calculate the relative density

In this example, we consider the case of the model combining the 'complete' ACT dataset (standardized data) and the LPO dataset (opportunistic data). For other examples of data combinations, see @Giraud2015.

First, we format the data for the fit.

Only the species monitored by ACT (`Species_in_ACT == 1`) contribute ACT counts: for the other species, the zeros in `X_ACT` mean "not recorded", not "absent", and must be left out.

```{r, eval=F}
inACT <- Aquitaine$Species_in_ACT == 1
df <- rbind(
  data.frame(species = Aquitaine$Species[inACT], site = Aquitaine$Site[inACT],
             N_obs = Aquitaine$X_ACT[inACT], effort = Aquitaine$Effort_ACT[inACT],
             dataset = "ACT"),
  data.frame(species = Aquitaine$Species, site = Aquitaine$Site,
             N_obs = Aquitaine$X_LPO, effort = 1, dataset = "LPO"))

# sites also surveyed by STOC, for species monitored by ACT: used to assess predictions
tabpred <- Aquitaine[Aquitaine$Site_in_STOC == 1 & inACT, ]
datapred <- data.frame(species = tabpred$Species, site = tabpred$Site,
                       effort = 1, dataset = "ACT")
```

The function `fun_abund_estim` allows to fit the model.

```{r, eval=F}
abund.mod <- fun_abund_estim(df = df, family = "quasipoisson")
#check the model summary 
summary(abund.mod$mod)
```


# Assess the predictive power of the model

If `newdata` is provided, the function `fun_abund_estim` allows to estimate the predicted values, and further assess the predictive power of the model.

```{r, eval=F}
abund.predmod <- fun_abund_estim(df=df, family="quasipoisson", newdata=datapred, type = "response")
#check the model summary 
summary(abund.predmod$mod)
#check the first predicted values
head(abund.predmod$N_pred)
```

Note that fitting the model on the full data set takes a few minutes (one parameter per species x site combination).

We then use `fun_pearsons()` and `fun_braycurt()` to calculate Pearsons and Bray-Curtis statistic values to compare predicted estimates (*N_pred*) and estimates from other estimation approaches (*N_ref*).

```{r,eval=F}
#estimate species abundance species with another approach
N_STOC <- tabpred$X_STOC/tabpred$Effort_STOC

#calculate Pearsons statistics
pearson.stat <- fun_pearsons(N_pred = abund.predmod$N_pred, N_ref = N_STOC, newdata = datapred)

#calculate Bray_curtis statistics
braycurt.stat <- fun_braycurt(N_pred = abund.predmod$N_pred, N_ref = N_STOC, newdata = datapred)
      
```
